title: The companions
hookLine: the people who walked with him
tomorrow: whose names are written in the front of Dadi's old Qur'an?

cards: Spend twenty minutes in a coffee shop and you carry it out with you: roasted beans in your hair, on your sleeve, in the car on the way home. You didn't buy a thing, and you still smell like the place.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ noticed the same thing, only his shop sold perfume. And he used it to say something about friends.

teach.h: THE PERFUME SELLER AND THE BELLOWS.
teach.b: Here's the hadith, in Bukhari and Muslim. A good companion is like a perfume seller: he may give you some, or you may buy some, or at the very least you walk away smelling sweet.
A bad companion is like a blacksmith's bellows: he may burn your clothes, or at the very least you walk away smelling of smoke. Company gets into you, whether you meant it to or not.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE WHO WALKED WITH HIM.
teach.b: Now look at the people who walked with him, the sahaba, the companions. Abu Bakr, his friend, hidden with him in a cave while they were being hunted.
The Qur'an keeps what the Prophet told him there: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us."
Bilal, who had been enslaved, and whose voice carried the call to prayer.
One to tell a friend tonight: when the words of the call were first taught, the Prophet asked that they be given to Bilal, because his voice carried further.
Khadijah, his wife, who believed in him when he came home shaking. Aisha, whose memory carried a great many of his words to the people after him. Ali, his young cousin, raised in his house.
Merchants, a freed slave, a widow, a boy.
What they shared was nearness. They walked beside him long enough to carry the scent home.
The Qur'an speaks of those who led the way and those who followed them in goodness, and says God is pleased with them, and they with Him.

how: Muslims honor the companions of the Prophet, the sahaba, often saying 'may God be pleased with him' or 'with her' after their names, and learn their stories in families, mosques and weekend schools.

o: the angels who carried the Qur'an to the Prophet
the people who knew and walked with the Prophet
the scholars who wrote down the law much later

games.q: who walked with him — tap the pairs.
p: the voice that carried the call
his wife, who believed in him

s: the companions of the Prophet were only men
Khadijah and Aisha were companions too, and Aisha carried many of his words to later people.
in the hadith, the bad companion is like a blacksmith's bellows
it may burn your clothes, or leave you smelling of smoke (Bukhari 2101).
Bilal was asked to give the call because his voice carried
the Prophet asked that the words be taught to Bilal for that reason (Abu Dawud 499).

games.q: at a new job, there's a lunch table that roasts everyone who isn't there, and a quieter one that doesn't. you like people at both. what does the perfume seller say?
o: sit anywhere; if your heart's in the right place, company can't touch you.
you leave smelling of the table you sit at, so choose with that in mind.
eat alone at your desk, since every table carries some risk.
games.why: the hadith says company gets into you either way: perfume or smoke. it doesn't say avoid people; it says notice what you carry home.

practice: Find something near you with a scent: coffee, a spice jar, soap, your own sleeve. Breathe it in slowly, and on each of the next five breaths, name one of the people who walked with him: Abu Bakr, Bilal, Khadijah, Aisha, Ali.
Then let one person from your own life come to mind whose company you carry home.

wordCard.voice: The companions: the sahaba, the people who walked with the Prophet, and carried what they learned home.

orig.note: Arabic: the companions, the people who knew the Prophet.

carryVoice: The line for today: good company, the kind you're glad to smell like on the drive home. Six of fifteen.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2101; Sahih Muslim 2628 (the perfume seller and the blacksmith's bellows)

sources.q: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.
